rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to a shallower slope. The current last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution while likely keeping all peaks within 10 minutes.

The limiting pair improved substantially with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the solvent window further reduces the slope, while raising the starting organic fraction should offset the extra retention and help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward by 0.05 to shorten retention while preserving the slope that resolved every pair. This should move the last peak clearly below 10 minutes, eliminating the small time penalty hidden by the rounded CRF.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. The 0.92-minute margin in the previous run should accommodate the added retention while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; now test a modest temperature increase to shorten the fully resolved separation. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates temperature’s effect on the critical pair.

Test whether a larger temperature increase carries the critical pair through an elution-order reversal and restores resolution while shortening retention. Injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback; this run explores a potentially faster selectivity regime.
At 60 C the central cluster separates, but a different pair nearly co-elutes. Test 55 C to seek a temperature window that resolves both groups while retaining most of the speed advantage over 40 C.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to improve the pair at R = 1.41 while monitoring the other close pair at R = 1.74. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves ample room for this modest increase in retention.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the maximum-score separation, with a slightly shallower slope to help preserve central-pair resolution. Monitor the first two peaks for excessive compression as their retention decreases.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve early retention and potentially separate the pair compressed by the higher start. A steeper gradient should offset the lower start and shorten the separation; monitor both central close pairs for retained resolution.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by two gradient minutes to test whether maximum CRF can be retained with earlier elution. Holding the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the slope response of the two close central pairs.

Lower the starting organic fraction to recover selectivity for the pair that lost resolution in the shorter gradient. Earlier runs suggest this can improve that pair despite a steeper slope, potentially retaining full resolution with the last peak before 8 minutes.

With maximum CRF already secured, explore a substantially faster gradient at 60 C. The troublesome middle pair may separate after an elution-order reversal, while the higher temperature previously improved separation within the later central cluster.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction widens the middle pair after its apparent order reversal at 60 C. Keep the short gradient to pursue full resolution near five minutes, while checking that neighboring peaks remain separated.

Explore low-temperature selectivity with a fast, broad gradient, since the high-temperature route trades one close pair against its neighbor. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, and the steep gradient limits the added retention at 25 C.

Test a steeper gradient at 60 C to increase separation of the middle pair on its reversed-order branch. Lowering the starting organic fraction should help protect the neighboring pair that was approaching the resolution threshold in injection 15.

Trim the unused high-organic portion of injection 13 while preserving its starting composition and gradient slope exactly. All peaks previously eluted before this shortened gradient ends, so this method should retain maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test the unexplored temperature just below 40 C using the original fast scouting gradient. This isolates whether modest cooling improves the central bottleneck without causing the extensive co-elution seen at 25 C, with maximum-score methods already secured.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 18 to probe the speed limit of the best fully resolved selectivity regime. This small change should shorten the last-peak time, though the two central pairs have limited resolution margin.

Seek a more robust maximum-score method by balancing the two central resolution margins at a slope between injections 11 and 12. This should remain near eight minutes while improving the narrow R = 1.52 margin of the fastest fully resolved method.

Slightly steepen injection 21’s gradient to shorten retention while aiming to retain both central pairs above R = 1.5. This tests an intermediate slope between the fully resolved injection 21 and the faster, partially resolved injection 12.

Probe the resolution boundary with a small slope increase from injection 22, targeting a last peak around 7.6 minutes. The limiting pair may fall just below R = 1.5, but this tests whether a slightly faster maximum-score method is available.

Preserve the slope and starting composition of the fastest fully resolved method while trimming the endpoint to just above the last peak’s estimated elution composition. All peaks should still elute during the gradient, retaining CRF = 1.000 and the approximately 7.60-minute last-peak time.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 9 to improve its limiting R = 1.59 pair while preserving the other close pair’s margin. This targets a maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins and an expected last peak below 10 minutes.
